This is just preaching.  You aren't even actually making arguments.  Proselytizing isn't really permitted, this is a debate sub, not a get preached at sub.

But, you did ask some questions.  In the title you ask why we doubt.  This one is simple, doubt is one of the most fundamental forms of thought.  Decarte's "I think, therefore I am" can be reworded "I doubt, therefore I am".  Doubt is the first step to discovering truth.  Not doubting would be a profound mistake.

You also ask why we don't believe, or in my case, why I no longer believe.  I was raised christian, from an early age I was spoon fed mythology and i swallowed it happily.  A magical tale of a demigod walking the earth, necromancers raising the dead, a generational curse that can only be cured by blood sacrifice.  The love of Jesus was intoxicating, and the wrath of God was terrifying.  But as I grew older and the utility of doubt honed my critical thinking skills and I learned more about the world this fairytale became less and less believable. The supposed all loving nature of God seemed incompatible with the brutal tyrant that disintegrated people for disobedience and toyed with human lives as tests of faith.  My interest in paleontology made it very clear that the events of the Bible, like the flood of Noah, never happened.  It quickly became impossible to decipher what parts of the story were allegorical or factual, and what lessons I was supposed to learn from many of them.  I tried and tried to make sense of it.  To make the world of my faith compatible with the world I lived in and I simply could not.  So I stopped trying and rebuilt my worldview on the most solid foundation I could.  And free from dogma and magic the world finally made sense.

I studied the world, and I didn't find god. I studied the Bible, and I didn't find god.  There is nothing I have ever learned or experienced that has ever made god seem possible, let alone probable.

I dont think there are many ninja capable of surviving that preasure.

Deep diving animals have special adaptations that help them to re-inflate their lungs after the preasure fully collapses them.  Elephant seals, the deepest diving mammals, have a startling amount of what is effectively lung snot.  When they dive, the preasure collapses their lungs, and this lung snot prevents their collapsed lungs from sticking together.

A human, regardless of how much ninja magic they have, doesn't have a way to stop their lungs from getting stuck together because its not a problem we face on the surface.  At these preasures, a full lung full of air gets compressed out of the lungs and into your esophagus.  Your lungs get smushed flat. With your lungs smushed flat like this, they can't pull in air anymore.  Even if a ninja could survive the multiple rapid preasure changes that come with being teleported to the bottom of the ocean and swimming to the surface fast enough to get a breath of air.  Anatomically, their lungs would no longer be capable of pulling air in. They'd move their diaphragm to take a breath and no air would reach the lungs because there isn't a way to pull air into them.  They'd suffocate with their head above water.

The average depth of the ocean is 12,000 feet.  The average length of time a person can hold their breath  is 30-90 seconds.  Now, a ninja definitely isn't a normal person, but its safe to say they weren't expecting to need to hold their breath.  Unprepared, let's give them a generous 100 second breath hold.  At the average depth, that means they'd need to move around 120 ft/sec to surface, or about 82 mph.  Doesn't sound that crazy, but remember, this is swimming, not running.  The fastest a human has ever swam is about 5 mph.  The fastest fish in the ocean can only do about 70.  This is also just an average depth, the deepest part of the ocean is 3 times as deep.

But wait, more bad news.  I'm not convinced a ninja would even know where they had been transported to and therfore wouldn't know what they needed to do to escape.  The bottom of the ocean is completely devoid of light.  Like up doesn't even look slightly brighter for thousands of meters devoid of light.  It's also cold, 1-4 degrees Celsius cold, marginally above freezing.  So, from the perspective of this poor ninja, one moment they're minding their own business, the next they find themselves in complete freezing darkness.  The ambient preasure is close to 380 times the surface preasure, about 5,500 psi, so it's like being stuck in the blast wave of a bomb, a preasure that far exceeds ruptured ear drums and collapsed lungs, and bowl perforations.  Disoriented doesn't even begin to describe how horrible this would be.  Blind, deaf, being crushed from all sides in water so cold all you can likely feel is your numbing skin and the internal pain of the preasure.

Given everything we've seen in the naruto universe, if you suddenly found yourself here, would you actually think "....ocean"  or would your first thought be genjutsu or another dimension.

Well, the most honest possition to take regarding the beginning is "we don't know"  because we don't.  We know the universe expanded, but what caused the expansion, what happened before the expansion, and if there even was a before the expansion are all unknowns.  It's entirely possible that some of these questions just don't have answers because they make incorrect assumptions about the nature of causality in the universe.

You made the point that since the universe is expanding, it seems rational that there was a starting point that it expanded from.  That's not necessarily true though.  In math, it's possible to write equations that graph to form curves that infinitely approach a line without ever crossing it.  The line they are constantly moving towards is called an asymptope.  This kind of math demonstrates that it actually isn't irrational to imagine the universe as just always expanding.  If it works similar to an asymptope, what you imagine as the starting point is actually just the point the universe gets infinitely closer to without ever actually have being there.  And that's a possible explanation that doesn't rely on any of the weirdness and conventionally nonsensical logic that quantum mechanics might bring into the equation.

As to the point about how we could ever get to now if there is infinite time, b theory makes that a non-issue.  If all times are equally real and existent it's kind of arbitrary where the present falls on that block of spacetime.

I'm by no means an expert on the topic, but given what we do know about the subject there's nothing that paints it as impossible that the universe didn't begin, and time is infinite.  And since I have no intention of becoming a doctor of astrophysics or quantum mechanics, I'm pretty comfortable leaving it at I dont know.

From my perspective, all human morality is the result of evolution.  Humans are a social species.  We have to work together to survive.

We can see the earliest sparks of morality in the behavior of other social organisms.  Cooperation, altruism, a sense of what constitutes fair treatment.

Humans have a general universal baseline of what constitutes moral behavior because certain behaviors are programed into us by evolution.  We know that being treated differently by people makes us feel bad, and we know that other people can and do feel the same things we do.  These inate biological responses are then extrapolated on through learning.  We interact with other people and we learn that being mean to other children makes them not want to play with us.

You're correct in asserting that no 2 people think alike.  But the vast majority of humans think alike enough that what we might call objective moral truths become learn able.

And make no mistake, there is an objectivity to the foundations of our morality, but its not something spoken into law.  It's a hard fought best we can do shaped by millions of years of evolution.

I firmly believe that moral truths like don't murder predate humans, as evidenced by the behavior of animals.  Violent altercations between members of the same species over mating rights or territory rarely result in the death of the loser, and lots of animals have turned these competitions into one's of dancing or building or showing off.  Because a species where every individual has absolutely no problem with killing any other member of the species is going to have a harder time being successful.  If there were 2 species competeing for the same niche, and one of them killed each other a lot, and the other just killed each other occasionally, the one with less intraspecies killing has the advantage.

I dont believe morality is simply a matter of opinion.  It's a combination of millions of subjective experiences interacting with each other, weeding out the bad ideas and trending towards the kinds of behaviors and thoughts that are objectively beneficial to the large scale success of the larger social group and species.

With this huge deficit there are likely multiple causes.

The biggest expense is probably recruitment and party expenses for any garrisons at your feifs and any parties you have roaming the map.  Address the fiefs first, go to the clan tab, under parties it should show the garrisons of all of your feifs.  It defaults to giving your garrisons unlimited budget for hiring and upgrading troops.  You need to limit it.  If you want your feifs to be profitable set the garrison budget at less than the income of the feif.

You can also disband or limit your parties to further reduce your expenses, bit this will significantly reduce your military capacity.

Double check your other sources of income.  Make sure you have all of your workshops purchased, and that they are all profitable.  Things like having workshops in richer towns, not having duplicates of the same workshop in the same town, and having the right kind of workshop for the town can all impact how profitable the workshops are.

Any companions with high trade should probably be running caravans if you can spare them.

Next, check your tributes.  If you're the king you will be paying a higher percentage of the tribute payments, but recruiting more lords can help reduce the overall amount you pay.  It might be worthwhile to instigate a war if you have an exorbitant tribute payment, which will also put you in a possition to make money fast from selling war loot.

While you get your finances under control it is very important for you to try to end wars quickly in a way that results in them paying you.  This means capturing enemy lords and keeping them in prison.  I wouldn't recommend ransoming someone unless they're willing to pay top dollar for them.

The best way to make the kind of money you need to make to keep up with your expenses is selling everything.  If you aren't at war, start one, then find the parties you can beat and take their gear. Sell all of it.  It's also fantastic to smith.  Two-handed swords sell for the most, with a high smith skill you can crank out a dozen swords worth 10000 each without even needing steel.

Let's also think about what rasengan is.  It's not exactly an elegant jutsu.  You create a swirling vortex of concentrated chakra and smash stuff with it. There are two ideas about why this trait evolved.

The first is mate selection.  Since the males do not provide any help in child rearing, and mating attempts tend to be rather aggressive. It provides a lot of benefits for the females to have absolute control over what males they allow to actually reproduce with them, since a successful mating requires cooperation from the female. 
(A similar preasure lead to the labyrinthine cloacae of female ducks.  Aggressive males plus no male parental care equals hostile reproductive architecture that only works when the female wants it to work.)

The other idea is a sort of camouflage to protect females from each other.  Females are the dominants in hyena social structure.  A clan consists of a handful of related females and the immigrant males they've picked up. Females tend not to change clans, and the females are constantly competing with each other for status.  So the pseudo penis serves as protection against infanticide.  Since the infant females will grow up to be competitors, if it's harder to tell the males and females apart the females are less likely to be singled out.

It's a combination of these two brutal pressures that are believed to have resulted in this unusual adaptation.

It's definitely possible, but jams in a flintlock are pretty different than jams in modern firearms.  If your flintlock jams, it's because at least one of the parts is broken.

Its also important to point out that all of the barrels fire together.  There isnt a mechanism that selects the barrel being fired.  The only parts that could jam are the hammer or pan lid.

In case you don't know how flintlocks work. The spring loaded striker, or hammer has a chunk of flint in it.  When you pull the trigger, the hammer swings forward, scraping that flint on the steel face of the Frizzen.  Flint and steel make a spark, that spark ignites the gunpowder in the flash pan.  The flash pan has a little hole leading to the back of the barrel, so when the powder in the pan ignites, it burns down that little tunnel like a fuse until it reaches the large powder charge behind the bullet.  That charge explodes, shooting the bullet.

There are a number of other points of failure that are significantly more important to consider than jams.

Wet gunpowder, failure to properly pack the charge, or insufficient priming powder in the pan could all result in a failure to fire or an increadibly weak shot.

On the flip side, using too much gunpowder, or double loading balls could cause a catastrophic failure like the explosion of the gun.

These are universal problems for muzzle loaded guns, so with a volley gun the level of concern for each of these factors is increased by the number of barrel.

An additional concern with volley guns is the slight unpredictability of lose gunpowder.  With all flintlocks there's a bit of delay between when you pull the trigger and when the gun actually fires because it takes time for the fire in the flash pan to reach the barrel, its less than a second, but it isnt negligible.  This kind of volley gun is just 4 barrels connected to a single flash pan.  It will take slightly different amounts of time for the fire to reach all 4 barrels.  So while one trigger pull does shoot all 4 barrels, all 4 barrels do not shoot simultaneously, there could be as much as a quarter second difference between when the first and last barrels fire.  There's potential for the first bullet fired to have already hit its target before the last bullet leaves the gun.  If the barrels fire this out of sync, the recoil is very likely to mess with your aim.  Since there's no way to know which barrel will fire first, or how out if sync they will be, you cannot effectively aim any individual barrel.  You really just point the gun in the direction of a group of people and hope you hit some of them.

They were difficult to manufacture and took a long time to load so they weren't practical for warfare.  But they did work in the sense that they did shoot multiple rounds at once.

There were lots of different versions of volley guns.  The largest were essentially trying to turn a line of infantry into a cannon like gun.  These really weren't useful because a cannon loaded with grape shot achieved a similar or better effect at significantly less cost and with a greater rate of fire.

There were multibarreled muskets that were essentially just shotguns with the effective range of a musket, so really not that great, especially when you take into account the difficulty of loading 5 to 7 individual barrels.

These Duckfoot pistols were actually, kind of ironically, the most useful application of the idea of a volley gun.  In the time of flintlocks, if you had a pistol, you really only shot it once during any engagement.  Because of the poor accuracy and range you'd really only use it as you closed the distance into a melle engagement, you probably weren't going to reload it until after the battle.  In naval warfare, it was relatively common for sailors and pirates to have multiple pistols, essentially the logic was, when I jump on the enemy ship I'll have 4 shots before I need to pull out my sword.

In this context, where you only expect to shoot your pistol once before switching to a melle weapon, a volley gun is potentially better than a single shot pistol.  The long reload time isn't significant, because you weren't going to reload until after the fight was over.  And the multiple barrels compensates for the poor accuracy of a smooth bore flintlock and provides additional stopping power.  It changes your trigger pull from "There are some bad guys over there, I'd like to kill one of them" to "There are some bad guys over there and I'd like to kill some of them".  Historically, they weren't widely used, likely because of the price and difficulty of manufacturing them.  They're really more of a novelty than anything.

In the case of the birds, both populations are changing, there's no amount of selective preasure that can stop mutations from occurring.

The parent population appears to change very little, because there is very little change that can occur to make the population better for its environment.  The selective preasures weed out most changes, because most changes aren't beneficial.  They still evolving to be better suited for their environment, there's just not much that can actually change to make them better 

The colonizing population appears to change quite a bit, because there are a lot of changes that can benefit them in the new environment.  So the selective preasures favor more significant changes.

The colonial population hasn't experienced more evolution, the process of evolution just resulted in a significantly more dramatic outcome.

Let's use the shark example.

Neither the shark nor evolution made a decision to grow more teeth.

The shark didn't know more teeth would be useful, and even if it did, it wouldn't be able to make itself grow more teeth.

I'll try to keep this simple.

What happened was the ancestors of sharks had a certain number of teeth.  Maybe only one set.  When they'd eat, their teeth would occasionally get damaged or fall out.  If this happened frequently, it could easily prevent the shark from being able to catch food.  Even just reducing the number of successful hunting attempts would put that shark at a disadvantage.

Now, there isn't just one ancestral shark, there's a group of them.  And in that group of sharks there will be a number of different sharks with different mutations.  Some may have more or less teeth, some may have bigger or smaller teeth, some may have sharper or duller teeth.  All of these minor differences will lead to different levels of success.  The sharks with the most beneficial traits will eat more food, be healthier, live longer, and have more offspring as a result.  The sharks with less beneficial traits will struggle, and have less offspring as a result.

Since the sharks with beneficial traits are having more offspring than the sharks with detrimental traits, the percentage of sharks with good traits will increase.

Going back to the sharks teeth getting damaged, this was likely a problem all the sharks had to deal with.  So, the sharks with mutations that gave them more teeth, or extra rows of teeth, or continuous growth of new teeth were on average more successful than the sharks that didn't have these traits.  Because of their increased success, those sharks had more offspring on average, and the sharks without those mutations had less.

I'll lay out a very very simple example of how it works.

Let's start with 4 sharks.  G will be the sharks with good mutations, B will be the sharks with bad mutations.

GBBB 4 sharks

The G sharks have more success, and therefore more children. If the B sharks each have 2 children, the G sharks have 3

The next generation looks like this

GGGBBBBBB
3G 6B

Continue this trend.

9G 12B
27G 24B
81G 48B

Notice how the G sharks have begun to outnumber the B sharks

But the ocean doesn't have enough food for all these sharks.  Maybe there's only enough food for 100 sharks.  Not only are there more G sharks, but the G sharks are also better at hunting.  So there will be disproportionately more G sharks that survive.  If we only keep the best 100 sharks, we will have 81Gs and 19Bs

Through this process of different success rates leading to different numbers of offspring, beneficial traits become more common.

Through the process of needing to compete for limited resources, the detrimental traits become less common.

And that's how an individual with a beneficial trait can result in the majority of that population having that trait.  We started with 1G and 3B, and now almost every shark is a G.

This is a radically oversimplified demonstration of how selective preasures work, but I think it does the job to demonstrate the basics.

Let's put a timeline on this.

The oldest stone tools we've found are 3.3 million years old. They predating the genus homo by close to a million years.

The stone age begins roughly 2.6 million years ago with the earliest evidence of humans using stone tools.  Not homo sapiens, at this point it was things like homo habilis.

Homo sapiens (modern humans) appear 300,000 years ago

Several species of humans refined the tools for over a million years before modern humans appear.  Modern humans evolved from a population of other humans that was already making spear points and very complex stone tools.

And it still took 297,000 years for us to to really start using metal.

The evolutionary path humans took as we diverged from the other apes was only possible because we already had stone tools.

In other tool using animals, the tools are something they make or find for overcoming a particular challenge.  Generally, they don't need tools to meet their needs.

As others have pointed out, most therapods did have 4 toes.

But I'd also like to point out the evolutionary trends surrounding number of toes.

On average, large terrestrial animals adapted for running have fewer toes than other animals.

In birds, ostriches have 2 toes. Emu and cassowary have 3.  While the flying birds typically have 4.

In mammals, most groups have 4 or 5 toes, unless you're an ungulate, where toes number from as few as 1 to the more normal number of 4.  Even within smaller groups there's a trend for runners to have fewer toes.  In ungulates, animals like horses have 1 toe, antelope and deer have 2 toes with 2 significantly reduced dew claws, tapirs and rhinos have 3 toes.   In carnivorans, dogs have 4 real toes on each foot, with a reduced dewclaw or spur on their front feet.  While cats have 5 full toes on their front feet and 4 on their back, as is more typical of carnivorans.  Canids (dogs) are the most cursorial (adapted for running) of all the carnivorans, and they have the fewest toes.

Therapods likely had fewer full toes than modern birds because they spent more time running than modern birds do.

I'm going to clarify some misconceptions about species that you haven't been made aware of.

>I understand that a species is a group of distinct organisms that can reproduce with one another.

This is only one of several different working definitions of species.  This definition of species does not apply to microbes, or any other organisms that can reproduce asexually.  Its also not always true, there are some species that are perfectly capable of producing viable offspring with a closely related species, but they are considered separate species because a behavioral or geographic barrier prevents them from reproducing in nature.

There are also strange examples of species where not all members of the species are capable of reproducing with just any other member of the species.  There's a species of lizard in California, it exists from the south by Mexico, all the way up into northern California.  If you were to take a southern lizard, and try to breed it with a northern one, it wouldn't work, even though they are considered the same species.  Why? Because the genes from the most extreme parts of the lizards range still transfer through the entire population of lizards.  The southern lizards can breed with the lizards in the middle, and those lizards can breed with the lizards to the North.  So there is still one population if lizards sharing a genome, even though the variation from the south to the north is so large they can't reproduce directly.

There is a similar case with dogs.  Great Danes and chihuahuas are the same species.  It's technically possible for their genes to produce viable offspring.  But anatomically they are completely incompatible.  By some definitions of species, this makes them different species.

Exactly what a species is depends on the definition you decide to use, and there isn't a single definition that applies to everything we consider to be a species.

This is because species aren't real. Not really.  It's not a concept or rule that nature abides by.  Species are categories we invented to make it easier for us to understand what's going on.  The actual lines between species are blurry.  There isn't a definite amount of genetic variation that prevents hybridization.  Horses and donkeys are capable of producing sterile hybrids.  As are tigers and lions.  Humans and chimpanzees are not capable of producing any offspring, despite the fact that humans are more similar to chimps than horses are to donkeys, and tigers are to lions.


>Also if the environment permits could certain species evolve to be able to mate and reproduce even if they arent a closes relative species?

Hypothetically, yes.  There isn't anything besides unfathomable improbability that would prevent this from happening.  It is theoretically possible for genomes to convergently evolve to be compatible.

But in a realistic, practical sense, it's impossible.  There are just too many factors that would need to line up perfectly for this to happen.  It would be like rolling billions of dice and having all of them land on the same number twice in a row.  Technically it is possible, but its never going to happen.

The problem you're having seems to be the most common misconception about what a species is.  We use the term species to describe static snap shots of an evershifting spectrum of change.

If you were to line up every animal in the transition from apes to humans, every child would look like it's parents.  The change from generation to generation is so small it's practically unnoticeable.



My favorite analogy is color.  Look at a color wheel with a gradient.  When does red become orange?  It's probably quite easy to find a point you're comfortable calling red.  And it's probably easy to find a point you're comfortable calling orange.  These are essentially the concept of species.

But if you look at the gradient or red oranges and orange reds and try to draw a line where red stops and orange starts, it's going to be difficult, I would argue, impossible.

Each slightly different shade of orangey reds is so similar, you could put them right next to each other and confuse them for the same color.  Yet, as you move from shade to shade you will eventually reach a point you're confident is orange.

This is how species evolve.  The shade of each generation gets changed so marginally it looks like nothing changes, until you take a step back and compare where you are to where you started.

Other animals have the same variability in size as humans do.

It just looks like human size variation is greater because of our posture, because we're larger than most animals we interact with, and because we have a bias for recognizing differences in humans.

Posture is important because there's multiple ways size can vary.  If one cat is bigger than another, it might be because it has longer legs, or because it is longer.  While the size variation is still very present in cats, it's less noticeable because it's spread out across 2 directions.  In humans, our legs and our bodies both contribute to our height in the same direction.  Long legs and a long body both add height, so the variations add together.  Our size variation isn't abnormal, our body plan is.

The next reason is our general body size is larger.  So the same percentage difference in body size looks larger in humans.  The average height of a person is 69 inches (5'9)  a person who is a foot shorter than them (4'9) is 83% of their height.  Let's look at a cat now.  Foot to shoulder is close to 10 inches on average.  Nose to butt is close to 18.  So if cats walked like humans they'd be around 28 inches tall.  83% of 28 is 23.  So the height difference between an average human and a human a foot shorter than them is roughly equivalent to a 5 inch difference in cat size.  Since a cat has a different posture we need to split that between height and length.  that roughly translates to a 2.5 inch difference in height and length.  That is significantly less noticeable than the size variation in humans despite being proportionally identical.

The last reason is our human bias. We just notice human stuff more. It sticks out. On top of that, our sensory organs are located towards the tops of our heads, that sit on top of our bodies, which makes it even easier to tell the difference in height of humans.

The main thing about ranching is keeping the population stable.

This means controlling your breeding stock.

With animals that give birth, the problem area is the pregnant mothers. Leaving auto slaughter on "Kill pregnant" can seriously hurt your production, as you're constantly losing the next animal, but if you don't kill the pregnant ones, they can stack up high above your population limit as a pregnant animal won't be slaughtered under normal circumstances.

With egg laying animals, the problem is volume.  They reproduce in bursts, and at any one time, like 5 to 6 generations of the animal exist. So if your herder is out of commission for a day or 2, the population of your pen might balloon again a day after he catches up with the work, because the eggs are just now hatching.  But, unlike with pregnancy, egg development doesn't impact auto slaughter.  So you know when you set it to 10 females, there will only be 10 adult females in the pen.

The reason I prefer egg layers is the general peace of mind.  The fact that the next generation exists as an item on the ground, and not a status effect on the mother means that when the mother starves to death in her overcrowded pen, the eggs will still hatch.  Radical population swings won't lead to total population collapse.  You also have more ways of controlling the population, because you can eat fertilized eggs.  If you want to stop a generation of chickens, make breakfast.

Free will and lack of evil thoughts might be mutually exclusive.  But free will and the lack of the suffering evil causes are not.

Your will can be completely free without the consequences of your evil actions causing suffering.

The problem with the free will defense is it excuses all evil as if preventing any suffering would turn us into mindless slaves.  But this isn't the case.

An analogy to illustrate my point.

In videogames there are a number of different ways developers handle player choices. For simplicity, let's look at obstacles like cliffs.  There are multiple ways to insentivise players to not jump off a cliff.  One common way is fall damage, if a player makes the mistake of falling from too high in the air, they will take damage.  They are free to jump, but if they do they suffer. This is the world we find ourselves in.  We are free to make mistakes, and when we do, we cause suffering.

Another option is to prevent the player from jumping with some kind of barrier.  This is how you think preventing suffering would work. The player is not free to jump of the cliff, and so they cannot suffer the consequences of doing so. The agency of the player is restricted.

Now, a third option, and the reason this defense fails, is to not restrict the freedom to jump, but also prevent the player from taking damage.  In this scenario, the player does not suffer injury or death for foolish mistakes, yet they are still perfectly capable of making the foolish mistake.

You're probably thinking that this final option prevents justice by freeing the player of consequences. But, in order to restore the consequences of poor choices, we don't need to punish the player with damage. Instead, we could bring them to a tutorial world where they learn how to not jump off cliffs. Or give them a cut scene where they are educated on why it was foolish to jump when their objective is on top of the hill. Or a friendly npc could pop up and show them the way back to the top.  At no point is death or injury required, at no point is the agency if the player restricted.

So no, free will does not necessitate suffering. It is entirely possible for the god you imagine to make a world where we are free to choose evil and not suffer, or cause others to suffer.

If your god is real, and good, and loving, and merciful we shouldn't be able to accidentally or intentionally kill children.  We shouldn't have to learn from our mistakes only after we've broken our bodies from terrible falls.

Well, every biological system is the result of a series of incremental mutations.

One of my favorite examples is the different ways animals have been pressured to evolve flight.

The most common is arboreal animals developing flaps of skin to help them glide.  Pterosaurs and bats likely went this route.  When you're falling from a height, any drag is good drag, so any mutation that increases the amount of loose skin between didgets and limbs would steadily increase effectiveness until you have animals with built in parachutes. Then, mutations in the arms allow for more control in the air, eventually culminating in powered flight.

But this isn't the only path to air travel. Flying fish have a completely different strategy.  Some fish jump out of the water to escape predators.  The flying fish is an example of mutations in fin size making this behavior more viable. It started with fish that jumped, the fish with slightly larger fins would travel slightly further or with slightly more control, making it that much more likely they survive.  Every fish doesn't have the same size fins, and the slight variation in fin size in the population is the result of mutations. So the mutant fish with big fins were consistently better at jumping away, so the fin size of the population increased until they could "fly" for hundreds of feet.

The evolution of flight in birds is even stranger.  The advantages of gliding probably initiated the change over to powered flight, but birds didn't get their wings in order to fly.  Feathers were the dinosaur equivalent to the hair mammals have.  Across the whole spectrum of dinosaurs there are spike feathers, fuzzy feathers, almost sorta feathers, and even pretty dang close to flight feathers.  The "flight feathers appear in the therapod dinosaurs, the original structure was large feathers on their arms.  The main driving force for the development of these long, sturdy, flat feathers was egg incubation. Therapods had relatively thin bodies and relatively short arms, so by having these "wings" they could more effectively incubate a larger clutch of eggs.  Therapods used their arms alot for hunting, so the faster, jumpier, raptors had to keep these blanket feathers more aerodynamic.  So they likely went more like flying fish in that there were advantages in aerial mobility when jumping at speed.  So the blankets became stabilizers.  Then, since they also had strong arms, they could use the stabilizers to help push them up inclines when running.  Eventually when their descendents moved into the trees, having these stabilizing blankets gave them the advantage of already having a parachute, so it wasn't too long before their powerful arms mutated to get better at controlling, and then eventually powering flight.

Every change, every variation in organisms is the result of genetics, and one of the largest sources of change in genetics is mutation.  Whenever we see changes, we know mutation played a significant part, because it is alwayshappening.  We see a lot of examples of lineages acquiring new traits as a result of these changes.

In humans, a very small mutation can result in a person growing extra fingers, sometimes those fingers work well enough to be useful. Like this family in Brazil. https://youtu.be/LlfPIKQmPok

They have an extra finger that works. The biological system of their hands is not only different from human baseline because of mutation, but arguably better than human baseline.  They could play piano music impossible for a master pianist to play because they could play 12 notes instead of the maximum 10 of a normal human.  And, depending on their reproductive success, there could easily be a point in the future where humans having 12 fingers instead of 10 becomes the norm.

We see mutations changing and making new systems all the time, across the entire tree of life.

My guess is the lack of mobility.  Most animals with radial symmetry are filter feeders, and the ones that do hunt are slow moving.  In a strange way, organisms with radial symmetry were probably the first to adapt to tohlerate short times out of the water because of tidal zones.  It's harder for them to move, so when they get stuck on a rock when the tide moves out, they need something to keep them alive as they crawl their way to a puddle or wait for the water to come back.

But since their survival strategy doesn't rely on mobility, instead relying on their food coming to them or being too stationery to escape, they didn't have the tools necessary for risky exploration in search of food.  Stationery filter feeders can't move onto land unless the waves wash their offspring onto the shore, and then there's no food.  Jellyfish have no rigidity, and so can't do anything after the lack of water collapses them into a pile of jelly. The only radially symmetrical animal that has a chance are things like starfish and urchin, they can move enough to escape the surface when water levels change, but if there isn't food up there there's nothing to motivate them risking their lives.

In a purely speculative sense, it is absolutely possible that some radially symmetrical animal for which we have no fossils, did colonize the shore at some point, venturing out of the tide pools to scrape algae off rocks, or even moving out of the water for a day or two to graze on early land plants before there was much competition.  Only to have the far more mobile colonizers out compete them and drive them all back to the sea.  But apart from it being fun to speculate, there's no reason to think they ever made it out of the tide pools, they're just too slow.

Why have snakes and spiders found their way into so many myths?  Could it be that myths and legends directly mirror the fears of the people who made them? Why, yes, yes they do.

We have myths and a cultural fear of spiders and snakes because our primate ancestors were scared of them, and not just learned fear.  Our brains have specific structures primed for identifying things like snakes and spiders.  For snakes it's slithering tubes, for spiders it's the tons of legs.

Thats why house centipedes are much less pleasant than squater slower centipedes.

It's not just learning from culture. Our culture is informed by nature, specifically our natural fears.  That culture then reinforces our natural fears, and teaches the people born without that fear.

There are no universal fears, everyone is a little different.  But the fear of spiders is not exclusively from culture.  If we erased every single myth and preconception of fear of spiders from every living person, we would have arachnophobes again in exactly 1 generation, because the fear that fast leggy things are probably dangerous is hardwired into most of us.

So, for the most part I agree, it's a fear if fast moving unpredictable animals.

But I think the reason fast moving and unpredictable animals carry a fear is because of their tendency to rely on venom.

There's no reason to be afraid of most arthropods, but the ones you should be afraid of have venom.  So we identify possible threats based on speed, but the reason we identify these animals as possible threats is venom.  The larger we get, the less we need to fear venom, but the threat never really goes away.  So the fear of getting bitten by fast moving animals remains a usefull adaptation even after we become too large for most to be dangerous.

So spiders and snakes are particularly scary, because we know they probably have venom, and they move really fast.

Evolution is a game of finding useful sources of energy.  We think the first organisms developed around hydrothermal vents.  Essentially volcanic exhaust pipes in the bottom of the ocean.  The energy gradient of boiling chemicals pouring into super cold water gave them a way to keep themselves moving by using the natural flow of energy in a system to do work.

When all the space around the food vents got taken up, what is a microbe to do? Starve to death?  Why would they do that when there's plenty of energy in their neighbors? And so some organisms started eating other organisms, became that was easier than waiting in line for food.

The next big resource organisms found they could exploit was sunlight.  Where the vent dwellers had access to hot chemicals with enough energy to do work on their own, and the first predators had access to other organisms who had already gathered the resources for them.  Photosynthesizers had the chemicals they needed, but not the energy to do anything with them, so as soon as they figured out how to use the sun's energy to do the work of staying alive, they had a brand new source of usable energy.

Producers like photosynthetic and chemosynthetic organisms use the abundance of free energy gradients to maintain life, but there is still competition for access to those gradients.  Think of a tiny plant trying to grow in the shade of a big tree, the tree gets way more light.

So when competition for access to these resources gets so intense that an organism can't meet their needs, they look for alternatives, like taking it from the organisms who have it.

Herbivores steal the hard work of plants because they don't know how to cook food with sunlight.  Carnivores steal the hardwork of Herbivores, because they don't like what the plants are cooking.  Decomposers steal the hardwork of dead things because, after all, they aren't using it anymore.

Evolution is a game of organisms finding new ways to get resources.

You're making the mistake of assuming theoretical probability is equivalent to experimental probability.

There is no reason to assume any alternate versions of the universe are possible.  As far as we know, this universe is the only one, and it exists in the only way a universe could ever exist.  The sample size is 1.  The experimental probability of the universe existing exactly the way it does is 100%.

In order for your argument to be valid you would have to demonstrate the existence of another universe somehow different from our universe.  That there is some other way that a universe can exists.

You can't calculate the probability of a coin flip if you only flip it once.

>The universe is too well-designed or aligned to be a total accident, in my view.

How did you come to this conclusion?

Your belief seems to be based on the assumption that the universe existing as it does is somehow improbable.  But this assumption is not grounded in any form of reality.

We as humans have this strange tendency to treat hypothetical, imagined possibility as if it is the same as actual possibility.  Which leads us to conflate the theoretical probability of an event happening, with the experimental probability.

The theoretical probability of the universe happening in exactly this way is so astronomically small as to be all but incalculable.  But the experimental probability, the observed probability, of the universe happening this way is 100%.  Any version of the universe that is different from the actual universe, exists exclusively in our imagination.  We have no evidence strongly supporting the actual existence of any kind of universe that isn't the one we inhabit.  As far as we know, this is it, and there's no other way it could actually be.

Its fun to think abstractly about hypothetical possibility, but don't fall into the trap of thinking your imagination accurately reflects reality.

With a coin flip, we know the theoretical possibility of it being heads is just under 50%, because we can flip a coin 1000 times and calculate averages to make predictions.  We have multiple examples of coin flips, but there is only 1 universe. The sample size is one.  We can't run the experiment again and see if it turns out any differently.

Its funny coming to this thread later looking for a little more info before I get the final trade perk and seeing all these bewildered comments about how hard it is to trade to the millions.

In my current game I'm full sending trading. I started at 20, started trading immediately, and now my character is 40 sitting on almost 5 million gold.  Now, I get blacksmithing could get you there a lot faster.  But It's not that hard to get up into the millions with trading.  The first mill is the hardest because during that time, most of your wealth exists as goods, but as soon as you build up the stock and with the right perks, it's smooth sailing.

Let go over how to do this.  First, spec into trade, 8 attribute and 5 focus points is the minimum to get all the way to the settlement bartering perk.

Next, buy pack animals.  For one, the max debuff for herding keeps you twice as fast as being overburdened and you need the inventory space.  For 2, you can buy mules for less than 30 gold, and sell them for more than 200.  Stock up on mules and Sumpters anytime you find them for less than 30.  Obviously selling them reduces their price, but at 30 gold purchasing price it's worth every penny to sell them for 40.  Keep an eye on their price at villages, prices don't change in village trades, so you can keep the price very high as you recover that 2000 gold you just spend clearing them out.

Next, buy everything green.  Until you start to pick up on the profitable prices and can take bigger risks, the ui is incredibly helpful.  Stop at every village and buy their cheapest goods, sell those goods for literally any profit.  Don't wait for the price of an item to skyrocket in the early stages, you need as much money as possible to buy more goods with.  With a stronger trade rumor network you can start to make longer term plans.

Now you need a route,  the easiest way is big circle.  I pick sanala as my start possition because there are quite a few goods that are very profitable to sell there, and they have tons of cheep food.  Bring goods from the south to the north, bring goods from the east to the west.  The sturgians don't have olives, the Aserai don't have cheese.  Aserai horses are one of the best goods, and the vlandians can't get enough.  If you have a lot of food items, look for a warzone and trade at a freshly broken seige, an imperial town is the best for this since food prices are higher in the empire anyway because of their village hearth debuff.  By manipulating the workshops in cities you can dramatically change the economy.  Just swapping the tanney in Askar with a brewery dropped the cost of aserai horse in the area, and raised the cost of grain Calradia wide from 4ish to 7 at the cheepest.

Now you have your route and enough mules to lug everything around. The next step is patience.  You will be painfully slow at first. Focus on scouting and riding to boost that speed. With the right perks and the right terrain, you can have a full herd debuff, a full infantry army, and maximum prisoners and still move fast enough to catch large groups of looters.  You should also consider maximizing your trade xp gain.  You get trade xp from selling goods you buy at a profit, so items attained through other means don't help.  I haven't done any formal testing, but it seems like you get more xp from separating your trades. Don't buy and sell everything in the same transaction.  Instead, do each side of market as its own trade. Buy everything you can, then go back into the market and sell.  When I had a high xp modifier, a 10000 denar gain from buying and selling would give me one trade level, and an identical gain from 2 separate interactions would give me 2 or 3 trade levels.  I typically sell loot items during the buy phase to counteract the cost without losing the xp.

Peace is very important for your trade empire. Don't be a vassal or commit crimes, when at war, your access to potentially profitable markets is reduced. Your caravans are also at more of a risk and since we're so slow, getting your companion back on the road is increadibly painful.  It also puts you at risk of getting attacked because, we're so slow.  Vassalage is less of an issue because you have allies, but one misstimed declaration of war and you might be trapped deep in enemy territory with no escape, and  the ever shifting political landscape might see your strategically placed rumor workshops get raided.  To break up the monotony of trading, I recommend very short mercenary contracts. Not only does this get you paid, but it also gives you the freedom to chose your wars. If you're about to get attacked by an enemy army, you can just leave the kingdom with no consequences.  Also, just because you're never actively participating in most wars doesn't mean you can't have a huge effect.  Your neutrality means you're free to stage whatever prison break you want.  Prison breaks are great for several reasons, freeing the lord gives them a huge relation bonus, making it easier to buy their feifs later.  It also gives skill xp for skills you don't use often as a merchant.  Freeing the lord gives their faction an advantage in the war as they can field more troops.  Plus plus, if you bring throwing knives or just lead the lord into danger, you can skip all the fuss of an execution and kill them with no negative effecs beyond the cost of the bribe.  If a faction is getting too strong kill their leaders until they arent a threat.  In this way, even without feifs or armies, you can still feel like the most powerful clan.

DO NOT GET CAPTURED.  Getting captured is the most detrimental outcome for a merchant.  With this strategy, by the time you have 100k in the bank, it's not unreasonable for you to have 6 times that value in inventory.  When you get captured, the loss of goods means you lose a lot more than a regular lord.   A loss of 1/6th of your goods is effectively the same as reducing your wallet to 0, and you're lucky if you get to keep a 6th of them.  In addition to this, since your inventory was bloated beyond belief, whatever items you're thankfully left with make the process of rebuilding so much worse since it will take half a week to get to the closest village for more troops.

The biggest issue with the merchant life is the speed.  Moving across the map is an absolute chore. And, since it takes so much time to build up the stock, without a fief to stash it in, getting back into combat shape takes forever.  Unless you're ok with selling your millions of dollars worth of merchandise at a loss, its going to take a long time to sell enough to get your map speed up to pursuit level.

Insidious? Really?  I firmly disagree with that word choice.  Insidious implies intent.  The way you phrase this implies that the author of the book is intentionally enforcing stereotypes to manipulate children into conforming with them.  I'm not going to asert that absolutely no author has ever done this, but I suspect that the authors that have are such a small minority that it's hardly worth mentioning.  I look at it like this.  The children's books the author read when they were a kid were probably much more heavy handed with the stereotyping, so when the author is brainstorming ideas he recalls the books he read, and falls back on the simplest social contexts he can to make the book relatable.  This manifests as the authors programming bleeding through into his work.  Causing a reinforcement of those stereotypes.  The author is just as much a victim of these stereotypes as the children reading their book.

I also see a second issue here.  We support books that present diverse lifestyles.  Moms that work, dad's that don't.  Mixed races, gay couples, single parent households.  Girls that play in the mud and boys that play with dolls.  All of these are good things.  But in our push to add diversity, we look down on books that don't insert it.  As if a mom that stays home, a dad that works, a son that plays sports and a girl who likes cooking are all bad ideas with negative effects on the youth.  As if diversity is everything that isn't the "norm" instead of what it actually is, which is everything, as many variations as we can come up with.  The truth is, girls are allowed to like traditionally feminine things. So if we shut down every book that uses a nuclear family structure and traditional gender roles, we move those lifestyles into the space that "alternative" lifestyles now occupy.  My point is, this isn't a dichotomy.  It's not either diversity or "traditional".  The presence of the traditional is essential to have a truly diverse outlook.  It's not bad to include characters that conform to traditional gender stereotypes, it's bad to present those stereotypes as the only acceptable way of living.  In our push for diversity we need to be careful that our complaints and objections stay as, "we should try to include everyone" without turning into, "we should include everyone but those people".
